newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary panel ends meeting on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary panel ends meeting on single currency.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee ended the first of a two-day meeting on Tuesday to discuss a budget stability pact among countries joining a single currency and related issues, sources said.
No information was immediately available of how the talks progressed, with officials due to resume their discussion on Wednesday morning.

The regularly scheduled gathering comes amid renewed doubts over how much agreement there is on the details of a stability pact, designed to enforce budgetary rigour among governments taking part in European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Under the plan, governments running deficits in excess of three percent of total output would face an initial fine of 0.2 percent of GDP, with a further one percent of GDP penalty tacked on for every percentage point over the three percent threshold.
A maximum fine of 0.5 percent of output is envisaged.
EU monetary officials say Germany is expected to stand firm against a perceived watering down of its initial proposal.

In particular, Bonn is worried that governments might escape punitive sanctions should their economies suffer an economic downturn. A precise definition of what constitutes a recession is what Germany wants, sources said.
German officials also want the fine to be open-ended.

The European Commission, in its draft proposal for a stability pact last month, shied away from quantifying such exceptional economic circumstances due to strong resistance from several commissioners.
Officials now say agreement on a budget accord is unlikely before next year, with some expecting only a political declaration by EU leaders when they meet in Dublin on December 13-14.
The committee will also contemplate the economic outlook for the 15-nation bloc with reports by the Commission and the European Monetary Institute forming the basis for discussion.
Rounding out the session will be further work on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, linking the single currency to countries on the perimeter of EMU, and legal issues regarding monetary union.
